title: Missing values and honest cleaning
goal: Find missing entries and choose a treatment that fits the question.
prerequisites: You can convert columns and use Boolean masks.

cells.title: Missing is not the same as empty or zero
cells.explanation: `isna()` gives True where a value is missing. Zero is a recorded value, and an empty string is text unless you explicitly treat it as missing. Counting True values with `.sum()` counts missing entries.
cells.code:
values = pd.Series([0, None, "", pd.NA, np.nan], dtype="object")
result = values.isna()
print(result.tolist())
print("Missing count:", result.sum())

questions.prompt: What type of values does `isna()` return?
questions.answer: True/False values, one for each entry.

questions.prompt: How many missing entries will be counted?
Why is the empty string not automatically missing?
questions.answer: It is a stored text value. A cleaning rule must say whether blank text represents missing data.

cells.task: Treat the empty string as missing, but keep zero. Store the cleaned Series in `result` and count missing entries.
cells.solution:
values = pd.Series([0, None, "", pd.NA, np.nan], dtype="object")
result = values.replace("", pd.NA)
print(result)
print("Missing count:", result.isna().sum())
cells.solution_note: Four values are now missing. The recorded zero is still zero.

check.prompt: Which original value is known rather than missing?
check.feedback: Zero is a numeric value; it should not disappear just because some data are missing.

cells.verify: assert result.tolist() == [False, True, False, True, True]
cells.watch: Use `.isna()`, not `== np.nan`, to detect missing values.
cells.takeaway: Define what missing means in your dataset.

cells.title: Drop rows only for required fields
cells.explanation: `dropna(subset=[...])` removes rows missing the specified fields. It does not remove a row just because an unrelated field is missing. Keep a count of excluded records and consider how the exclusion affects the answer.
cells.code:
df = raw_students()
df["Score"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Score"], errors="coerce")
result = df.dropna(subset=["Score"])
print(result[["Student_ID", "Score", "Study_Hours"]])
print("Rows kept:", len(result))

questions.prompt: Which column controls row removal in this cell?
Will S006 remain even though Study_Hours is missing?
questions.answer: Yes. S006 has a score, so it passes the Score-only requirement.
It may remove rows for fields the analysis does not need, changing the sample unnecessarily.

cells.task: Keep only rows with both Score and Study_Hours available. Leave the intentional duplicate for the next module.
cells.hint: Pass both required column names to `subset`.
cells.solution:
df = raw_students()
df["Score"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Score"], errors="coerce")
result = df.dropna(subset=["Score", "Study_Hours"])
print(result[["Student_ID", "Score", "Study_Hours"]])
print("Rows kept:", len(result))
cells.solution_note: Ten rows remain out of thirteen. S004, S008, and S006 were excluded for the stated requirements.

options: The fields that must be present
The first few rows to show
check.feedback: Only missing values in those columns trigger removal.

cells.solution_verify:
assert len(result) == 10
assert not set(["S004", "S006", "S008"]) & set(result["Student_ID"])
cells.watch: Removing incomplete records can change the composition of your data; report what was excluded.
cells.takeaway: Match required fields to the analysis question.

cells.title: Fill a label without inventing a measurement
cells.explanation: `fillna()` replaces missing values with a value you specify. A label such as "Unknown" can make a missing category visible in a report. The same idea does not justify inventing a score or age.
cells.code:
campuses = pd.Series(["RAK", None, "Dubai", None], dtype="string")
result = campuses.fillna("Unknown")
print(result.tolist())

questions.prompt: What is being filled here: a measured number or a category label?
How many Unknown labels will appear?
Does Unknown tell us the actual campus?
questions.answer: No. It makes the missing information explicit; it does not recover the campus.

cells.task: Use the same Series, but first record a Boolean Was_missing flag. Store a DataFrame named result with the filled Campus column and the Was_missing flag.
cells.solution:
campuses = pd.Series(["RAK", None, "Dubai", None], dtype="string")
result = pd.DataFrame({"Campus": campuses.fillna("Unknown"), "Was_missing": campuses.isna()})
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The flag preserves which labels were originally missing, even after every cell contains text.

options: To restore information about which entries were filled
To prove the missing values were incorrect
check.feedback: After filling, the flag distinguishes observed labels from replacements.

cells.watch: Do not use zero as a universal replacement for missing numbers.
cells.takeaway: Keep missingness visible when replacements are used.

cells.title: Compare a fill policy with keeping missing data
cells.explanation: Preview of Module 16: the groupby, transform, and named aggregation syntax in this cell will be explained there. First focus on the difference between a technical replacement and a justified data policy. A group median is one possible imputation rule, not a universal answer. `transform()` returns a group result for every original row. This small example compares a proposed fill with the original values so its effect is visible.
cells.code:
df = pd.DataFrame({"Program": ["AI", "AI", "AI", "IT", "IT"], "Hours": [4.0, 8.0, np.nan, 2.0, np.nan]})
group_median = df.groupby("Program")["Hours"].transform("median")
result = df.assign(Hours_filled=df["Hours"].fillna(group_median), Was_missing=df["Hours"].isna())
print(result)

questions.prompt: Why does transform return five values instead of two group summaries?
questions.answer: It repeats each group median on the rows belonging to that group.

questions.prompt: Which values fill the missing AI and IT hours?
questions.answer: AI gets 6.0, the median of 4 and 8; IT gets 2.0, its only observed value.

questions.prompt: Why is filling the IT value with 2.0 a weakly supported choice?
questions.answer: It is based on only one observed IT value and can hide uncertainty or reduce apparent variation.

cells.task: Use the same original table. Keep the missing values and store a summary in result with Program as its index. Name the known Hours count Known_hours, the row count Rows, and the median Median_hours.
cells.hint: Use named aggregation; count counts known Hours, while size counts rows.
cells.solution:
df = pd.DataFrame({"Program": ["AI", "AI", "AI", "IT", "IT"], "Hours": [4.0, 8.0, np.nan, 2.0, np.nan]})
result = df.groupby("Program").agg(Known_hours=("Hours", "count"), Rows=("Hours", "size"), Median_hours=("Hours", "median"))
print(result)
cells.solution_note: AI has 2 known values in 3 rows; IT has 1 in 2. The report shows the missing information rather than replacing it.

check.prompt: Should every missing measurement be filled with a mean or median?
options: Only when the policy fits the context and its effects are checked
Only if the column is first converted to text
check.feedback: Choose and document a treatment; retaining missing values or excluding specific rows may be more appropriate.

cells.verify:
assert result.loc[2, "Hours_filled"] == 6.0
assert result.loc[4, "Hours_filled"] == 2.0
assert result["Was_missing"].sum() == 2
cells.solution_verify:
assert result.loc["AI", "Known_hours"] == 2
assert result.loc["IT", "Rows"] == 2
assert df["Hours"].isna().sum() == 2
cells.watch: In predictive modeling, fit any imputation rule on training data only; do not learn it from held-out test data.
cells.takeaway: Explain the assumption behind every fill policy.
